records.text: National Consumer Law Center.
I also testified before Congress twice during
hearings, once in front of the Senate Banking Committee
and once in front of the House Financial Services
Committee --
THE REPORTER:  Sorry, can you slow down just a
little bit there?  Once in front of the...
THE WITNESS:  I'm sorry.
Once in front of the Senate -- I --
Senate Banking Subcommittee in a hearing on student loan
servicing, as well as in front of the
House Financial Services Committee in another hearing in
2019 on student loan servicing.  Those were both done in
my capacity at the National Consumer Law Center.
Q    Ms. Yu, in -- in any of your work experience,
have you ever dealt with a situation where one loan
servicer takes over a student loan portfolio from another
loan servicer?
A    Yes, that -- that is a frequent occurrence.
Q    What has -- what has been your experience in
doing that?  What -- how many times has that come up?
A    So it does not -- I would say it's happened
about -- in the federal student loan context, it certainly
happens about a dozen times.  Most recently, we saw a
number of federal student loan servicers leave.  Navient
left and their loan portfolio transferred over to --
Q    Ms. Yu, you're starting to go fast again.
Apologies.
A    Sorry.
Most -- so most recently we saw, for example,
Navient left the Department of Education's loan portfolio,
and the loans were transferred to the company Maximus,
which runs a servicer called Aidvantage.  The -- PHEAA,
the loan servicer which operates under the name
FedLoan Servicing, also left the federal student loan
market.  Their loans were transferred to the servicer
Mohela.
There have been other smaller loan services which
have also left the market and which has resulted in
transfers of loan servicing to various different entities.
Also, loans are sometimes transferred from time to time.
This is also -- you know, occurs in the private student
loan market as well; however, the -- those occurrences
tend to be smaller and less spectacular with fewer
millions of borrowers transferred at any given moment.
Q    Thank you.
Do you have any experience with any of these
transfers in the private student loan market?
A    I do not recall -- I do -- I do not recall large
market transfers.  There may have been some when
Sallie Mae transitioned to Navient.  But like I said, they
happen typically on a much smaller scale than on the
Federal Student Loan scale.
Q    Thank you.
And whether they happen on a small scale or a
large scale, have you ever been involved in the nuts and
bolts of how they transfer the data from one servicer to
the other?  Or are you at a more 30,000-foot level?
MR. BLOOD:  Vague.
THE WITNESS:  Yes, I -- so what I understand --
I -- I have -- I have talked to servicers and the
Department of Education about what that process looks like
insofar as what the impact is to student loan borrowers.
For example, what has often happened is that
these loans as they are packaged to be transferred have to
be condensed into data files; right?  So many of these
servicers have multitudes of ways of -- of holding their
data.  Sometimes there are entire platforms that are
transferred.
For example, in the Navient to Maximus case,
the entire -- the -- Maximus took over the entire
servicing platform.  Whereas, in the case of
FedLoan Servicing to Mohela, loans had to be packaged.
And so I don't know that it's quite 30,000-square foot,
but I am not involved in the day-to-day operation of these
loans.  But I do a -- I -- I have an understanding of how
these transfers work insofar as what data is lost from --
from the student loan borrower's perspective and the risks
to student loan borrowers that can occur during a student
loan servicing transfer.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Well, what are those risks?
A    The risks are that data loss.  There can be risks
of lost payments.  There can be risks -- risk of lost
communications between customer service representatives.
There can be the risk of lost files, that sort of thing.
I mean, basically, data is lost is -- is the main risk.
Also, there is often confusion amongst borrowers
about where to make payments, what they need to -- who
they need to interface with, as it is often quite opaque
to -- to the consumer who they should be discuss --
talking to about their loans at any given moment.
Q    And in your experience in dealing with the
student loans you've just described --
A    Yes.
Q    -- is it generally your experience that if one
student loan servicer stops servicing a portfolio, another
one will step in and take over?
A    That is -- that is generally how -- in my
experience, that is often what happens.
Q    Are you aware of any occasion when one student
loan servicer stepped away from servicing a portfolio and
nobody came in to take over the servicing?
Has that ever happened in your experience?
A    I am not aware of any instance where that has
occurred.
Q    Are you -- are you aware of any regulations that
apply to the manner in which student loan servicing data
is supposed to be transferred from the original servicer
to the follow-on servicer when there's a change in student
loan servicing?
A    There are a number of state laws that would
apply.  For example,
California State Student Loan Servicing Law I believe has
requirements about the data that must be transferred from
one servicer to another in -- in a -- when a transfer
occurs.  I believe that other states as well, but I don't
know them off the top of my head.
Q    Thank you.
In this case, of course, we're dealing with the
PEAKS loans that were in use at ITT; correct?
A    That's correct.
Q    Are you aware of any regulations that were
violated when the data was transferred by the original
servicer in this case, the Access Group, to my clients --
we'll refer to them as Vervent, but they were
First Associates at the time, in 2011?
A    Am I aware of any data that -- I'm sorry, can you
say that again?
Q    Sure.
Are you aware of any regulations that were
violated when the Access Group transferred the data for
the PEAKS loans to my client, Vervent, in 2011?
A    That's outside the scope of what I was asked to
look at in this case, and I don't have -- I don't have
access to the documents of what was transferred and
couldn't make an opinion about what rules were or were not
violated.
Q    Okay.  Have you ever had a job related to
criminal law?
A    Yes.  I was an intern at the
District Attorney's Office in 2002.
Q    Is that about the extent of your work experience
relating to criminal law?
A    I have had -- tangentially, I have had some
experience working with survivors of domestic violence.
Q    Okay.  Other than that, any other experience with
criminal law?
A    I volunteered at a teen court when I was an
attorney in Rochester.
Q    Okay.  Other than that?
A    Other than that, I do not recall any other
instances.
I served on a jury once.
Q    Have you ever had a job where you decided whether
or not someone would be charged with a crime?
A    I have not.
Q    What familiar -- familiarity do you have with the
RICO statute?
A    I -- I -- I am generally aware of the RICO
statute.
Q    Have you ever had a job where you helped
determine whether a RICO enterprise existed?
A    In my work as -- as a consumer attorney, the -- I
have been in a position to consider or to work with others
who have considered whether or not a RICO violation has
occurred.
Q    Have you ever had any experience with that in the
context of student loans?
A    These cases would have been under -- these would
have been student loan related cases.  That's my primary
area of expertise.
Q    And how many times have you done that?
A    A small handful of times.  Less than half a --
less than half a dozen.
Q    And when was the last time you did that?
A    I couldn't recall.
Q    Does that mean it was five to ten years ago?
More?
A    Within the last five to ten years, for sure.
Q    In your report that is attached hereto as the
first exhibit to the deposition, did you make any findings
about whether there was a RICO enterprise?
A    I was not asked to provide a legal opinion as to
whether or not there was a RICO enterprise.
Q    So you made no findings with respect to that
issue?
A    This was -- that was outside the scope of my
report.
Q    Go down to -- I'm going to go back into your
report.  So I'm here -- there's paragraph 8 here.  You see
we're on page 2?  And after paragraph 8 we no longer have
any paragraph numbers.  Was that a conscious decision?
A    That was not a conscious decision.
Q    Okay.  It happens.  I'm not trying to give you a
hard time about it.  I just wondered if there's some
significance, if like the first part of it was prefatory
and the rest of it was different somehow, but that was --
it just is what it is?  Okay.
A    That just is what it is.
Q    Okay.  Thank you.
You provide -- the initial background, you
provide an overview of higher education and for-profit
colleges.  You have some familiarity with the concept of
for-profit colleges in America, I take it?
A    I do.
Q    And there -- there's no law against for-profit
schools; correct?
A    That is correct.
Q    There's no law against making a profit either;
correct?
A    That is correct.
Q    Did you have any firsthand experience with what
the quality of education was like at IT&T -- ITT?
MR. BLOOD:  Did you say firsthand?
MR. PURCELL:  Yes.
THE WITNESS:  I never attended ITT.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Did you -- as -- as part of your -- of your work,
did you ever do anything that analyzed whether -- the --
the level of -- of education there?
A    So the -- so my area of expertise is in student
lending, and so the area that I would've examined with
regards to ITT is with -- with the debt that students
incurred.  So I did -- I -- I have both on individual
level -- I -- I represented individual borrowers and --
who have a -- I've represented a small number of ITT
students; however, my expertise has been looking more
broadly at ITT and about the systemic problems that have
been identified by regulators, by, also, Senate
committees, and so looked systemically at the issues that
have been raised by student loan borrowers in those
contexts and understanding the ways in which ITT has led
students into debt.
Q    Would it be fair to say that your view about ITT,
based on the -- the materials you've reviewed, is that in
many occasions the benefits of an ITT education were
outweighed by the burdens of debt that students took?
A    I'm sorry, can you ask that one more time?
Q    Sure.
Is -- is your view that on many occasions ITT
students received less of a benefit from the education
there than would be commensurate to the amount of student
debt they had to take on?
A    So it is my view -- or let me rephrase that.
Based upon my analysis of the materials that is
in -- both in the public domain and in the reports by ITT
and the reports that I have relied on, what it has shown
is that few students or -- very few students receive the
benefits that are promised to them by ITT which is what
led them to take on the debt in the first place.
Q    So it -- it's not your opinion that an ITT
diploma is worthless; correct?
A    Is...
MR. BLOOD:  Vague.
THE WITNESS:  Well, yeah.  I mean, I think I
don't really understand what you mean when you say that it
is -- is worthless.  I mean, the data suggests that, you
know, folks who attend a school -- that folks who attend a
for-profit college and get a diploma, such as that from
ITT, typically earn less than they did even with just a
high school diploma.
I think beyond that, there's also issues about
whether or not students complete their degree.  ITT and
other for-profit schools have extraordinarily high dropout
rates.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Uh-huh.
A    And so many of the -- a large -- systemically
large number of folks -- even if one were to say that
the -- the degree had value -- which I -- I don't -- what
I know is the data around earnings, and I know about the
data around retention.  I don't -- I'm not in a position
to say about the educational quality, for example.  But
I -- what I can say is about the economic outcomes of
students that attend ITT are typic- -- are -- are
statistically worse than many folks who did not attend
ITT.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Okay.  So I'm just trying to unpack that a little
bit --
A    Sure.
Q    -- because you -- you're talking about
statistics.
So what -- what statistics are you aware of about
how many -- what percentage of ITT students ended up
getting degrees as opposed to those who did not get
degrees?
A    If you'll -- I -- I'm going to refer to my report
because I believe that I have this date.  I believe -- the
Senate HELP Committee looked specifically at ITT and
looked at the retention rates at ITT.
MR. BLOOD:  Ms. Yu, the -- the senate what
committee?  I didn't catch that.
THE WITNESS:  The -- the -- I'm sorry.
The Senate HELP Committee:  Health, Education,
Labor, and Pension Committee.
MR. BLOOD:  Thank you.
THE WITNESS:  They did a report in -- they
released a report in 2012 which was based upon a two-year
investigation into a number of for-profit institutions.
ITT was one of those schools that it investigated.  As a
part of that investigation, it released data regarding the
retention rates of ITT.  And I'm happy, if you'll give me
a moment, to take a look and to pull up that number for
you.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Sure.
A    So it appears that I did not put the exact figure
of the retention rates in -- into my report.  It isn't
documented in the Senate HELP Report.  The other -- the
other metric besides retention that is important to look
at when -- when judging the quality of the degree and the
quality of -- on whether borrowers experienced -- or
students rather experienced a valuable experience is to
look at the default rates at an institution, and so ITT
had a notably high default rate which indicates that --
which is a good indicator that students were not getting
the value from which they -- the value of the education
which they were taking on the loans to get.
Q    Okay.  So a couple sort of big-picture questions.
One --
A    Sure.
Q    -- one is just, it -- it is not your opinion that
every degree from ITT was worthless; is that fair?
MR. BLOOD:  Vague.
THE WITNESS:  I have no way of -- of evaluating
every single degree.  What I have is looking at
market-wide data available about the outcomes of ITT
students.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Okay.  How about this:  If there is an ITT
student and they got a degree and made more than twice as
much as they made after graduating from ITT than before
they attended ITT, would you consider that to be an
unusual experience with an ITT student?
MR. BLOOD:  Vague --
THE WITNESS:  Well --
MR. BLOOD:  Vague.  Incomplete hypothetical.
Go ahead.  You can answer.
THE WITNESS:  Sure.
That would be an outlier experience.  If a -- if
a student were to graduate and -- and -- I'm sorry, I
don't remember the details of your hypothetical.
(Simultaneous speakers.)
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Sure.  I'll go back and ask it more simply --
A    Sure.
Q    -- with -- with the benefit of your answer.
So you're saying it would -- it would be atypical
if an ITT student graduated with a degree and also made
twice as much, if not more, than they made prior to
attending ITT after getting the -- the degree.
That would be atypical; correct?
MR. BLOOD:  Incomplete hypothetical.
Go ahead.
THE WITNESS:  So I think -- I mean, I think
still -- I -- I think the words that I used before would
still apply.  It would be an outlier.  And I think that
there's a number of different factors that one would
consider.
I mean, I know -- there's a -- there's a number
of different factors that go into the exact salary that
someone makes after attending a school.  Many of them have
very little to do with the school itself.  However -- so
that's why I think it's important to look at the aggregate
field and to look big-picture at what is happening
throughout the field.
Is there a single student who may wind up doing
better?  Sure.  But that student may have done better
without the degree from ITT regardless, which is why
individual anecdotes are not necessarily instructive of
what is happening in the field.  I think what's more
instructive is to look at these big-picture, you know,
graduation rates, retention rates.  The rates of -- of
default, for example.
So yes, there are -- there are going to be
example of students who make decent salaries, but that is
not necessarily an indication.  You have to look instead
rather at the bigger picture of what's -- what's happening
across the field.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Sure.
But when you -- when you've used the -- the term
"outlier" -- and you've used it a couple times -- what do
you mean by that?
A    It is not the typical experience.  The typical
experience is that ITT was a -- was a notoriously bad
institution that -- that used, you know,
flagrant misrepresentations about the quality of
education --
(Simultaneous speakers.)
THE REPORTER:  I'm sorry, I'm sorry, you need to
slow down a little bit, Ms. Yu.  The -- I lost you after
"flagrant."
MR. BLOOD:  Flagrant misrepresentations.
THE WITNESS:  Flagrant misrepresentations, thank
you.
So, you know, I -- I -- I think what is more
important to recognize is that across the field ITT is
